passage: I posted the trek photo at four. By five I had checked it eleven times, honestly I lost count. When it hit fifty likes I felt tall, like standing on a rooftop. Then nothing moved for an hour and my chest sank. Harsha, you know that feeling? At dinner my phone was under the table. Dad just said, "Are you enjoying that photo, or counting it?" No lecture. Then he added, "Fifty or five, you're still the one who climbed the hill." I didn't answer. Later I thought: I can't name ten of those fifty people. But the four friends who climbed with me didn't even click like, they sent me laughing voice notes. That was better than fifty. Sachin

qa.q: How many likes did the photo have when Sachin felt tall?
qa.a: The photo had fifty likes when Sachin felt tall.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when the likes stopped coming, and what shows it?
qa.a: Low and anxious; the chest sank and the phone went under the table at dinner.

qa.q: What could Sachin try next time after posting a photo?
qa.a: Put the phone away for a while and enjoy the trek with the friends who were there.

qa.q: How might Dad see Sachin's checking at dinner?
qa.a: With gentle concern; Dad asks whether Sachin is enjoying the photo or counting it, without lecturing.

grounding: A teenager feels proud at likes and low at silence, and a parent gently says numbers do not measure the person.

passage: I'm Mahima, and in our class Eshaan posts a short dance video every Friday. By second period the phone comes out under the desk. I sit right behind, so I see the screen. Last week it had two hundred likes by lunch and Eshaan was practically bouncing, showing everyone. This Friday the number stuck at thirty. Eshaan went quiet, refreshed again and again, and snapped at me for asking about homework. I honestly don't know if it was about the video. At break our teacher sat beside Eshaan and said, "Your video made me smile. Thirty or three hundred, it isn't a score for you." Eshaan shrugged, but I saw a small nod.

qa.q: How many likes did the video have by lunch last week?
qa.a: The video had two hundred likes by lunch last week.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling when the number stuck at thirty, and how sure can Mahima be?
qa.a: Disappointed and low, judging by the quiet and repeated refreshing, but Mahima does not know whether it was about the video.

qa.q: What could a friend add to what the teacher said?
qa.a: Invite Eshaan to talk or dance together offline, showing that the friendship does not depend on numbers.

qa.q: Why might the teacher have sat beside Eshaan at break?
qa.a: To speak gently and privately, without embarrassing Eshaan in front of others, and to show the number is not a score.

grounding: A teenager who posts and refreshes feels proud at likes and low at silence, and an adult gently says numbers are not a measure of a person.

passage:
Saturday, 10.40 pm
Posted my painting of the flyover at sunset at 6. Two hours of work, plus the week of sketches. First hour: 11 likes. I felt amazing. I checked while brushing my teeth, while eating, during dinner under the table. By 9 it was still 23. Pooja from class got 200 for a picture of her new shoes. I hate that I checked hers.
Around 9.30 I nearly deleted mine. It felt like proof that I'm boring.
Samir mama saw me refreshing and asked to see the painting. Not the phone, the actual paper. He looked for a long time and asked how I got the orange to glow. I explained the wet-on-wet thing. He said, "Twenty-three strangers pressed a button. I just spent ten minutes looking. Which counts more?"
I didn't delete it. Still checking though. Sharmila, stop.

qa.q: How many likes did the painting have by 9?
qa.a: It still had 23 likes by 9.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel around 9.30, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sharmila felt low and worthless, nearly deleting the post and calling it proof of being boring.

qa.q: What did Samir mama do that helped?
qa.a: He asked to see the actual painting and asked how it was made, showing real interest and gently pointing out that likes are not the real measure.

qa.q: How might Samir mama have felt watching Sharmila refresh the phone during dinner?
qa.a: He was probably concerned and a little sad, seeing how much the numbers were hurting, which is why he turned attention to the painting itself.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who refreshes a post, feels proud at likes and low at silence, and an adult who gently shows numbers are not a measure of worth.

passage:

qa.q: How long did Ganga practise the turn?

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling about the reel with 4 likes?

passage: Madhav's kabaddi raid had been perfect: two touches, a dive, a clean escape back over the line. His cousin filmed it behind the Barsana bus stand, and Madhav posted it that evening with loud music. Next morning, on the way to school, he checked the phone every thirty seconds. Eighteen likes. Then nineteen. By lunch he was proud and sick at the same time, because a boy from the next village had three thousand for a scooter wheelie. Madhav stopped talking during games period. Sarika ma'am, the PT teacher, noticed him sitting on the steps staring at the screen. She sat down with her whistle still around her neck. "Show me." He showed her. "Nice ankle hold," she said. "Now show me the part where you lost the last raid." He laughed despite himself. "Tomorrow," she said, "you teach the juniors that escape." He did.

qa.q: Where did Madhav's cousin film the kabaddi raid?
qa.a: Behind the Barsana bus stand.

qa.q: How was Madhav feeling by lunch, and why?
qa.a: He felt proud and sick at once, pleased with his raid but deflated because another boy's video had thousands more likes.

qa.q: How did Sarika ma'am support Madhav?
qa.a: She looked at the actual skill, joked about the lost raid, and gave him a real task, teaching juniors, that showed his worth outside the likes.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika ma'am to see Madhav on the steps staring at his phone?
qa.a: She probably felt concerned, seeing a usually lively player go quiet, and wanted to steer him back to what he is actually good at.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who checks likes and feels low at a small number, and an adult who gently shows that numbers are not a measure of a person.

passage: In Singapore, Chen posted a photo of the drawing he had spent all weekend on, a heron over the canal, and then refreshed the app every two minutes through dinner. Eleven likes. Then nothing for an hour. His chest felt heavy. At nine he deleted the post. His uncle Diego, visiting from Manila, found him on the balcony. "Where's the heron? I wanted to show your aunt." "I took it down. Nobody liked it." Diego raised an eyebrow. "Eleven people liked it. And so did I, and I don't even have an account." Chen almost laughed. "It's not the same." "I know. But the drawing didn't get worse between eight and nine. Only the number changed." Chen took out his sketchbook and looked at the heron again. It was still good.

qa.q: How many likes did Chen's post get?
qa.a: It got eleven likes.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when he deleted the post?
qa.a: Chen felt low and disappointed, his chest heavy, as if the silence meant the drawing had no worth.

qa.q: How did Diego help Chen see the likes differently?
qa.a: Diego gently pointed out that the drawing didn't change, only the number did, separating Chen's work and worth from strangers' clicks.

qa.q: How might Diego see Chen's heron drawing?
qa.a: Diego clearly admires it, wanting to show it to Chen's aunt, and liked it without needing any app at all.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager whose mood rises and falls with likes, and an adult who gently shows that numbers do not measure a person or their work.
